questions.q: Define "conflict" in the context of a short story and name the two opposing forces in the independence vs. care conflict in *Vitamin-M*.
questions.a: Conflict is the central struggle between opposing forces that propels the plot. In *Vitamin-M*, the two forces are Grandpa's determination to live autonomously (independence) and his family's efforts to safeguard his well-being (care). A wrong answer that only says "Grandpa vs. family" without naming the *values* (independence vs. care) shows the student sees conflict as mere interpersonal friction rather than a clash of principles.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Grandpa's refusal to use a walking stick is not just stubbornness but a symbolic act in the independence-care conflict.
questions.a: The walking stick represents Grandpa's acceptance of frailty; refusing it signals his refusal to define himself by his limitations. He equates the stick with dependence, so rejecting it is his way of asserting, "I am still me." A student who calls it mere stubbornness misses the symbolic layer and cannot connect the action to the larger theme of dignity in aging.

questions.q: In the scene where Vidya hides Grandpa's house keys, apply the concept of "external conflict" to explain how this action escalates the independence-care tension.
questions.a: Step 1: Identify the external conflict — character vs. character (Grandpa vs. Vidya). Step 2: Note Vidya's intention (safety) and Grandpa's perception (control). Step 3: Show escalation: Grandpa's angry search for keys proves he feels trapped; Vidya's guilt shows she knows she crossed a line. Step 4: Conclude that the act transforms abstract worry into a concrete power struggle. A wrong answer that only describes the event without labelling it "external conflict" or linking intention vs. perception fails to apply the literary term.

questions.q: Analyse how the author uses *parallel scenes* — Grandpa's morning walk alone vs. the family's frantic search — to deepen the reader's empathy for both sides of the conflict.
questions.a: The solitary walk lets us experience Grandpa's joy in autonomy (sensory details: cool breeze, familiar streets), while the search scene immerses us in the family's panic (short sentences, repeated "Where is he?"). Juxtaposing these perspectives forces the reader to hold two truths: independence is life-giving; care is life-saving. A student who only summarises one scene cannot analyse the structural empathy the author builds.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the story's ending — Grandpa agreeing to a weekly check-in call — is a genuine resolution of the conflict or a temporary compromise. Justify with textual evidence.
questions.a: It is a compromise, not a full resolution. Evidence: Grandpa says, "I'll call *if* I remember," retaining conditional independence; Vidya smiles but still sets a phone alarm, showing lingering anxiety. The conflict's core — dignity vs. safety — remains alive, which is realistic for aging families. A student who calls it a "happy ending" ignores the nuanced, open-ended tone the author crafts.

questions.q: Create a 6-line dialogue between Grandpa and Ravi that captures the independence-care conflict without using the words "independence" or "care".
questions.a:
Grandpa: "I've walked this lane for forty years, beta."  
Ravi: "And the potholes have grown deeper in forty years, Papa."  
Grandpa: "My legs know every crack."  
Ravi: "My heart skips a beat when you're late."  
Grandpa: "Then walk *with* me, don't follow me."  
Ravi: "Deal. But I'm carrying the water bottle."  
A poor answer uses abstract nouns ("I need independence!") instead of concrete, character-specific details that show the conflict through action and subtext.
